text.en: A torch lights when we press the switch and goes off when we release it. Behind that is a complete path for electricity called a circuit.

An electric cell is a source of electricity. Several cells joined together make a battery. A circuit has a source, wires, a switch and a device like a bulb. Electricity flows only if the circuit is closed, a complete loop. An open circuit has a gap, so no current flows.
Circuits are drawn with symbols: a long line and a short line for a cell, a circle with a cross for a bulb and a break in the line for a switch.
Materials that allow current to pass are conductors, such as copper, iron and aluminium. Materials that do not are insulators, like rubber, plastic and wood. Wires have a metal core and a plastic cover for safety.
In a series circuit the bulbs are joined one after another. If one bulb fuses, all go off. In a parallel circuit each bulb has its own path. If one fuses, the others stay on. House wiring is parallel.
Never touch electric wires or switches with wet hands, and never put anything in sockets. Use only cells for experiments, never the mains.

problem.en: Why does the bulb not glow when the switch is open?

text.en: The loop is incomplete, so no current flows.

prompt.en: Why is the house wiring in parallel?

requiredIdeas.en: One fault does not turn off everything.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking a battery is one cell.

points.en: A circuit needs a complete loop.
Conductors allow current; insulators do not.
Series: one path; parallel: many paths.
